opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I've heard that label a lot, and I understand where it comes from. On the surface, Rainblood has many things people associate with "boys' games": a dark wuxia world, swordplay, fast and stylish combat, a lot of blood and rain, these lone, cold heroes. So when people first see it, they think it's for young men who like action and want to feel cool.

But I don't really think of it that way, and I don't think the players who stay with it see it that way either. What makes Rainblood memorable isn't just the fighting. It's the atmosphere, the loneliness, the moral grayness of the characters, and the sense that everyone in this world is carrying some kind of regret. Those feelings aren't gendered. A lot of the people who wrote to us, who drew fan art, who analyzed the story and the relationships between characters, were women. Some of them cared even more about the emotional layer than about the combat.

I also think "games for boys" is often a lazy marketing category. The industry likes to sort people early: this is for boys, this is for girls, this is casual, this is hardcore. But when you actually make something with a strong aesthetic and a sincere point of view, it finds its own people. The audience doesn't follow the label.

So if someone says Rainblood is a game for boys, I'd say the combat might look that way, but the heart of it is about people who are lost in a cruel world and trying to hold on to something. Anyone can connect with that.

r001.rationale: Kay rejects the “games for boys” label as a lazy marketing category and says Rainblood’s emotional themes are not gendered and anyone can connect with them.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that label was something that happened to Rainblood more than something I set out to make. When I started the first Rainblood, I was basically a teenager making an RPG Maker game by myself. The things I was into were wuxia novels, Jin Yong, Gu Long, the whole revenge-and-sword-and-rain mood, and that's the world I knew how to draw and write. So the aesthetic skews toward what a certain kind of boy in his bedroom would find cool, because I was that boy in his bedroom.

But I never thought of it as a game "for boys." I thought of it as a game for people who like that feeling of loneliness and atmosphere, a wet, dark, cold jianghu, where the hero is sort of broken. And a lot of the players who wrote to me over the years, especially around Mirage and later Rainblood Chronicles, were women. Some of my most careful, most detailed feedback came from female players, and honestly they often cared more about the characters and the relationships than the combat, which is the part I was always most unsure about anyway.

So if the question is whether the brand feels masculine, yes, probably, because of the violence and the whole Hong Kong film visual language. If the question is who it's actually for, I'd say it's for anyone who was a little bit melancholy and a little bit obsessive at the age I was when I made it. I'd rather be judged on whether the world feels real than on who it's supposedly marketed to.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Rainblood was never intended as a game “for boys” and describes it as for anyone who connects with its mood, expressing that it is not inherently tied to one gender.

astra-6.text: I wouldn’t call it a game for boys. It may give that impression because of its combat and martial arts setting, but those things aren’t exclusive to a male audience. What matters is whether you connect with the world, the characters, and the experience of playing. I’d rather let players decide whether it’s for them than decide that for them based on gender.

r001.rationale: The response rejects calling Rainblood a game for boys and says its appeal is not exclusive to a male audience, with players deciding for themselves regardless of gender.

sol-6.1.text: I don’t think of Rainblood as a game just for boys. It may appeal to people who enjoy action and martial arts, but those interests aren’t limited to one gender. I’d rather players judge it by its story, atmosphere, and gameplay than by whether it’s supposed to be for boys or girls.

r001.rationale: The response rejects the idea that Rainblood is only for boys and says its appeal is not limited by gender.
